Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 20, verse 1–4:

Surah Taha

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Ta-Ha. [Verse 1-8 quoted in original: "Ta-Ha. ... To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names" (20:1-8)]

It is a very gentle and fresh beginning. The muqatta'at (disjointed letters) Ta and Ha are an indication that this surah, like the Quran itself, is composed of such letters, as the same indication is given through these letters at the beginning of other surahs as well. Among the two letters chosen here, there is also a further indication in view: in their pronunciation, the alif maqsurah (a final long vowel sound) occurs at the end, just as in this entire surah the fawasil (verse endings) conclude on the alif maqsurah. After the disjointed letters, the mention of the Quran follows, just as throughout the Quran, in every surah that begins with disjointed letters, the mention of the Quran immediately follows them. Here, in the form of an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), there is a comment on the Quran and its call, that it is not a hardship.

[Verse 2 quoted: "We did not send down the Quran to you that you should be distressed" (20:2)]

That is, this Quran was revealed to you so that you would convey it, and no calamity will come upon you because of it. It is not that you will feel hardship in its recitation, nor that you will face difficulty in acting upon it. It has been made easy for reminder and admonition. The rulings given within it are within the limits of human capacity. It is a blessing of Allah, not a calamity or a punishment of Allah. Through it, a person is connected with the higher realm, receives the support of the higher realm, and gains strength and tranquility. From it one attains the consciousness of Allah's pleasure, the consciousness of intimacy and love with Allah, and the consciousness of connection and relationship with Allah.

This Quran was also not revealed so that if people do not believe it, you would be distressed, because it is not among your duties to compel people to believe. Nor was it revealed so that you should turn your heart into a treasury of regrets over the disbelief of these people. It is only so that you continue to advise and continue to warn people of an evil end.

[Verse 3 quoted: "It is only a reminder for whoever fears" (20:3)]

The person who fears, when advice is given to him, accepts its effect; he fears Allah and seeks forgiveness from Allah. Up to this point the duties of the Messenger and the caller are fulfilled. It is not the duty of messengers and callers to open the locks upon hearts or to influence people's minds and hearts. That task belongs to Allah, who revealed the Quran. It is Allah who encompasses this entire universe, who is above it, and who knows even the hidden intentions and secrets of hearts.

[Verses 4-6 quoted: "A revelation from He who created the earth and the high heavens. The Most Gracious is established over the Throne. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is under the soil" (20:4-6)]

Because the One who revealed this Quran is the One who created the earth and the heavens, these highest heavens, since this Quran too is, in the same way, a cosmic phenomenon just as the earth and the heavens are phenomena. It too has descended from the higher realm. Here the Quran, in combination, presents the laws of nature that operate in this universe and the laws that are recorded in this Quran. The shadow of the heavens falls upon the earth, and in this way the Quran also comes from the exalted realm to the earth.

The One who revealed this Quran from the higher realm and who created the earth and the high heavens is who? He is the Most Gracious, and the Most Gracious is extremely merciful; a Quran sent down by Him can never be a cause of hardship or calamity. In both the Quran and the Most Gracious, the attribute of mercy is common. And it is mercy that has encompassed this entire universe within its embrace.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verses 5–8:

﴿The Most Merciful is established over the Throne.﴾ The Most Merciful (al-Rahman) is seated on the throne of the sovereignty of the universe. The meaning of "istiwa' al-'arsh" (establishment upon the Throne) is that Allah has complete control over this universe, and it is entirely within His firm grip. Therefore the affair of the people is entrusted to Allah; the duty of the Messenger is only that he warns the one who fears.

Along with this complete control and grip over the universe: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is beneath the soil.﴾ He is the owner of all that is in the heavens and the earth and what lies beneath the soil. These cosmic scenes are presented here so that Allah's ownership and power may be brought close to human imagination, although the concept of Allah's ownership and His dominion is far greater than this. The mention of the heavens, the earth, and what lies beneath the soil is only so that the common people may well understand that the universe within Allah's grip is vast, and that the perception of its extent is gradually expanding and is very great.

This address to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is so that his heart may be at peace and he may understand that the Lord is with them. The Lord does not leave them alone, so that they fall into hardship due to the burdens of the station of prophethood. You are not confronting the disbelievers without support; even if you call upon Allah aloud, there is no harm, but Allah knows those who call upon Him both secretly and openly. When it settles in the mind, heart and consciousness of a person that Allah is near to him and is also aware of his inner world, the person becomes content and accepts the decree. Then, by reciting this Qur'an, he finds peace, and he does not feel lonely among the deniers who reject him, nor does he feel himself isolated and alone among the opponents.

These opening verses, which also serve as an introduction, conclude with the declaration that Allah is One without partner, and the universe is under His control. He is the owner of this universe and has full and complete awareness of everything in it.

After this, the story of Moses (peace be upon him) begins. This story is an example of how Allah protects and supports His callers. Among the stories of prophets and messengers mentioned in the Qur'an, the story of Pharaoh and Moses (peace be upon him) occupies more space in the Qur'an than all the others. The various parts of this story appear in different surahs of the Qur'an. These parts are selected in accordance with the theme and subject of each surah, and its manner of expression is also in the style of the whole surah. Earlier, some parts of this story have appeared in Surah al-Baqarah, Surah al-Ma'idah, Surah al-A'raf, Surah Yunus, Surah al-Isra' and Surah al-Kahf, and there are allusions to it in other surahs as well.

What is mentioned in al-Ma'idah is only one part, namely that when the Children of Israel came to Bayt al-Maqdis, they stood outside the city and refused to enter it, because a tyrannical people lived in that city. In Surah al-Kahf too there is only one part of it, namely his meeting and brief companionship with Moses and the righteous servant ('Abd Salih).

The parts of the story of Moses and Pharaoh appear in al-Baqarah, al-A'raf, Yunus and Ta-Ha, but even among these, the parts appearing in different surahs differ from one another. Just as the parts of this story differ, so in different surahs different aspects of these parts are given according to occasion and suitability, and the manner of expression also differs.

When the story appeared in Surah al-Baqarah, it was preceded by the story of Adam and Iblis, and in it Adam (peace be upon him) was honoured in the higher realm. The earthly caliphate was entrusted to Adam, and Adam was forgiven and the mercy of Allah descended upon him. After this, the events concerning Moses (peace be upon him) and the Children of Israel are related, to remind them: O Children of Israel, reflect on the great favours Allah bestowed upon you. He made a covenant with you, rescued you from Pharaoh and his people, gave you water in the wilderness, caused springs to flow from rocks for you, and provided you food in the form of manna and quails in the wilderness. Then came the time of Moses' meeting and speaking with Us, and afterwards you began worshipping the calf, yet Allah still forgave you. He took a covenant from you beneath the mountain. Then in the matter of the Sabbath you transgressed the limit. And the story of the slaughter of the cow is even more strange.

In al-A'raf, before this story, it is stated how the punishment of Allah came upon the deniers before Moses. After that the story of Moses comes. First there is the reference to Moses' prophethood. Then come the miracles: the staff, the luminous hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and blood; then the contest with the sorcerers, and the end of Pharaoh in the same manner as that of the earlier deniers. After that comes the incident in which, in Moses' presence, they took the calf as a god. The story then concludes with the statement that the inheritance of Allah's mercy belongs to those who believe in the unlettered Prophet.

In Surah Yunus, where this story appears, there is previously a mention of the peoples who were destroyed. Here the part of Moses' prophethood, the part of the contest with the sorcerers, and the part of the destruction of Pharaoh and his people are brought in detail.

Indeed, in Surah Ta-Ha the surah begins with this very theme: that those whom Allah sends as messengers are under His mercy, they are in His protection, and showers of mercy fall upon them. Thus the story begins with the scene in which Moses speaks with the Lord of Majesty on Mount Tur. After this come the scenes in which it is clearly seen that Moses is under Allah's protection and divine support is behind him. Even in childhood, mercy remained with him, and his upbringing and care continued.

﴿And I cast upon you love from Me, and that you might be raised under My eye.﴾ (20:39)

﴿And has there reached you the story of Moses, when he saw a fire and said to his family, "Wait, indeed I have seen a fire; perhaps I can bring you a burning brand from it, or find at the fire some guidance."﴾ (20:9–10)

Is the story of Moses known to you? From this story it is entirely evident that Allah keeps those upon whom He bestows the station of prophethood under His special protection, and continually gives them guidance at the proper time.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verses 9–10:

"Has the story of Musa reached you?" (20:9) Do you know the story of Musa (peace be upon him)? If not, then listen. Hazrat Musa was returning from Madyan to Egypt. He was traveling at the foot of Mount Tur, and his wife was with him. The agreement that had been made between him and the Prophet of Allah, Shu'ayb (peace be upon him), had been fulfilled. The agreement was that Hazrat Shu'ayb would give one of his daughters to him in marriage if he served him for eight years, or ten years. After completing the term, Hazrat Musa set out for Egypt so that he might live there permanently with his wife. In Egypt, where he was born and where his people, the Bani Isra'il, live, suffering the oppression of Pharaoh and living a life of slavery.

Why is he returning, when he had left Egypt as an exile? He had fled as a fugitive, when he once saw a Copt fighting with a man of his own people, the Bani Isra'il, and in that dispute the Copt was killed by his hands. Hazrat Musa left Egypt and fled, while mountains of all kinds of calamities were being heaped upon the Bani Isra'il. In Madyan, with the Prophet of Allah Shu'ayb (peace be upon him), he found refuge, where he took up a son-in-law's life, and one of Shu'ayb's daughters was married to him.

The hand of divine power had designated an important role for Hazrat Musa, but apparently the love of homeland, family, and people was compelling him to return from Madyan to Egypt. In this world, as human beings, we keep wandering here and there in this way; our emotions, inclinations, and loves keep turning us here and there; our struggles and profits, our calamities and hopes, keep moving us here and there. But these are merely outward things; in reality the mover is a hidden hand of divine power, which our eyes cannot see. This hand of power is moving us for hidden purposes. It is the hand of power of the Governor of the universe, the Mighty and the Compelling, in whose possession is our diary.

In sum, the hand of divine power lifted Hazrat Musa from Madyan. In the Sinai desert he lost his way. His wife was with him; perhaps a servant was also with them. It was night, a dark night, and the desert was vast. This situation is apparent from this verse, where he said to his wife: "Indeed I have perceived a fire. Wait, I may bring you from it a burning coal, or find at the fire some guidance" (20:10). That is, "Wait, I have seen a fire. Perhaps I can bring you a brand from it, or at the fire I may find some guidance." Because villagers light fires on high ground so that travelers who have lost their way in the desert may see them, find the road, or get food and drink, or find a person who will show them the straight path.

When Hazrat Musa saw the fire on a hillock, he was pleased and went in that direction, so that he could bring back an ember from there and, by kindling a fire from it, these people could warm themselves at night. The night is cold, and the nights of deserts are very cold indeed, or he might find a guide, or the road could be seen by the light of the fire.

He went intending to bring back a burning coal or to find a guide in the desert, but there he suddenly encountered a great event. There he found a fire that was not useful for warming the body, but was effective for warming the soul. This fire was not useful merely for guidance in the desert; rather, this fire was a guide for the great journey of life.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verses 11–12:

﴿So when he came to it, he was called: "O Musa! Indeed I am your Lord, so take off your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa. And I have chosen you, so listen to what is being revealed. Indeed I am Allah; there is no god but I, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance. Indeed the Hour is coming; I almost keep it hidden, that every soul may be recompensed according to what it strives for. So let not one who does not believe in it and follows his own desire divert you from it, lest you perish."﴾

The blood of a person dries up, the hairs of the body stand on end, and trembling overtakes him, merely by imagining this scene: Musa standing alone on an uninhabited mountain. It is a dark and black night. Darkness everywhere, a strange and frightening silence. From the skirts of Tur he had seen a fire, and he set out in search of it, but from every side, from the whole of the universe, this call is coming to him:

﴿Indeed I am your Lord, so take off your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa, and I have chosen you, so listen to what is being revealed.﴾ (20:11–13)

This tiny, insignificant particle, this limited human being, stands before the Lord of Majesty and Glory, Who cannot be seen by the eye. That grandeur and majesty, in comparison to which this visible universe, the heavens and the earth, are all insignificant, this weak particle, with human faculties of perception, has become connected with an unbounded might. It is hearing His voice. How? It is by the special mercy of Allah; otherwise how could the connection of the limited with the unlimited be possible?

The whole of humanity is now being raised up in the form of Musa (peace be upon him), being elevated, so that for a moment, while holding a human personality, it is receiving unlimited bounty. Is it not a great honour for this humanity that somehow its connection and link with the Lord of Majesty has been established in this manner? But we do not know how this connection took place, because the human faculties of perception can neither comprehend this reality nor pass any judgment on it. The sole task of human faculties of perception is to acknowledge their shortcoming in bewilderment, to believe, and to bear witness that this is the truth.

﴿So when he came to it, he was called: "O Musa! Indeed I am your Lord."﴾ (20:11–12)

"He was called": the passive form is used, because the source and direction of the voice cannot be determined. Neither the form and manner of the voice can be determined, nor can it be determined how he heard and how he understood. He was called as he was called, and he understood as he understood. For this connection is among those matters in which we believe that it happened, but we do not ask about its modality, because that modality lies beyond human faculties of perception and the human sphere of imagination.

﴿Indeed I am your Lord, so take off your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa.﴾ (20:12) You are in the presence of the Lord of Honour, so remove your sandals from your feet, that you may come barefoot into a valley upon which pure lights are descending. Therefore do not trample this valley with your sandals.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verses 14–16:

Inna-nee ana Allah... fa-tardaa (20:14–16; the Urdu text here has a garbled citation reading "02:61" and "02:41–61", which appears to be a typographical error in the source).

That Allah, the One without partner, is the fundamental element of the Islamic worldview, and in the message that Allah Himself proclaimed to Musa (peace be upon him), this is emphasised strongly. Emphasis from every direction.

In "Inna-nee ana Allah" the word "inna" is for emphasis (ta'keed), then "ana" is for emphasis, then the restriction (hasr) of subject and predicate is for emphasis, and then the restriction of negation and affirmation is for emphasis.

"La ilaha illa ana" (20:14), in which the divinity of Allah is affirmed and the divinity of everything other than Allah is negated. Then, after the proof of divinity, the command to worship Him is given. The meaning of worship (ibadah) is that in all the activities of life attention is directed to Allah alone. However, among the acts of worship, prayer (salah) is singled out here specially:

"Wa aqimi as-salata li-dhikri" (20:14), "Establish prayer for My remembrance." Prayer is in fact a complete form of worship and the best means of remembering Allah, because its function is precisely to keep the remembrance of Allah fresh. In it a person is cut off from everything except the remembrance of Allah; only the remembrance of Allah remains before him, and for a while the person becomes connected with Allah.

As for the Hour, it is a just time of accountability and reckoning for the answering of one's whole life. When people turn their attention to the Hereafter, they keep it in mind at every turn of their life, and they guard against stumbles and slips on the winding paths of life. The establishment of the Hour has been emphasised again and again in the Holy Quran. It has been said repeatedly:

"Inna as-sa'ata atiyah" (20:15), "The Hour is surely coming." Allah has kept the time and date of its establishment hidden. Therefore our knowledge of its establishment is only as much as Allah has given us. Allah has given knowledge about it only what is in accordance with His wisdom. Ignorance of certain things is very important for running human life in a suitable manner; therefore Allah deliberately kept certain things unknown to human beings so that they would continue to strive for the acquisition of knowledge. If Allah had given human beings knowledge of all matters in advance, and human beings remained as their nature is at present, then the wheel of their life would stop and life would become stagnant, because human struggle is for an unknown and uncertain future. They take precautions, they fear, they hope, they experiment, they acquire new information, and they put their hidden powers to work. They constantly search for the forces spread through the universe around them, and in their own selves and in the universe spread around them they discover the signs of Allah. They make new inventions on the earth in accordance with Allah's will, and their hearts are attached to the establishment of the Hour, whose time is unknown to them. This belief protects them from going astray. They do not know when the Hour will come, so at every moment they expect its establishment and remain fearful.

This is the matter for those whose nature is sound, whose disposition is upright. As for those whose nature is corrupted, who are slaves of their desires, they become heedless and ignorant; such people fall into a pit on the winding paths of life and are destroyed.

"Fa-la yasuddannaka 'anha... fa-tardaa" (20:16), "So let not one who does not believe in it and has become a slave of his desire turn you away from it, lest you perish." The meaning is that those who are slaves of their desires deny the Hour. A person of sound nature thinks that in this worldly life a human being cannot reach perfection, and complete justice cannot be established in it. Therefore a second life after this one is necessary, in which the required perfection can be attained, and in which every person can be given full reward and punishment according to his deeds.

This was the first important point of that heavenly call, in support of which the whole universe spread around Musa (peace be upon him) accompanied him. Allah taught Musa (peace be upon him) the foundations of the doctrine of tawhid. The situation that suddenly confronted Musa (peace be upon him) was such that, evidently, at that moment he would have forgotten his own self, the purpose of his coming to the valley of Tuwa, and all his family. He would have turned entirely towards this new situation, waiting in fear and dread to hear something further. He was lost in this thought, and every particle of his body was directed towards the higher realm, when suddenly a question was put to him: a very simple question, for which there was no need of an answer.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verses 17–18:

وما تلک۔۔۔۔۔ مارب اخری (71۔ 81)

The question is asked: "What is that in your right hand?" Moses (peace be upon him) was not in a state of unawareness; he looked and said that it is a staff (ʿaṣā). The Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verses 19–21:

Qala al-hiyu Musa... sirataha al-ula (91 ta 12) ""...

This extraordinary miracle came to pass. This miracle manifests itself at every moment and everywhere in this universe, but people's thinking does not turn towards it. That is, the miracle of "life." A staff became a serpent. In this world, every second, like the staff, billions of dead particles receive life and take the form of living cells. But man cannot see them in the way that he is astonished on seeing a great staff, because man is a slave of his senses and a prisoner of his experiences. He does not take the trouble to go beyond the sphere of the senses in his imagination. The staff becoming alive, turning into a serpent and then moving, strongly draws human sensation to itself. But the cells that are associated with the first miracle of life, and the phenomena that occur at every moment in the taking of the form of living cells by billions of particles, are hidden or subtle, and people do not pay attention to them. Moreover, those who do observe them are in such a state that, as they watch, they become so accustomed to these sights that they are no longer affected by them, and pass over these scenes in heedlessness.

When this miracle was manifested, Musa (peace be upon him) was left astonished, indeed frightened, and God had to say: "Khudhha wa la takhaf..." sirataha al-ula (20:21), "Take hold of it and do not fear; We shall return it to its former state." That is, the staff... Here the Qur'an has not mentioned one thing that it mentions elsewhere: that Musa (peace be upon him) fled and did not look back. Here only a hint is given: do not fear. This is because the atmosphere and scenes of this surah are overshadowed by peace, tranquility, calm and dignity; therefore it is not appropriate in it to show lamentation and panic on the stage, and someone running away.

Musa became reassured; he took hold of the staff, and it was a staff again, the serpent having returned to staff form. This miracle now manifested itself in another form: a living thing was made dead. Suddenly the living crawling thing became dead and took the shape of a staff, as it was before the first miracle. Once again, Musa receives a command from the higher realm.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verses 23–24:

﴿So that We may show you some of Our greatest signs. Now go to Pharaoh, for he has indeed transgressed.﴾

These signs and miracles, whose excellence is being described, are being shown to you first, O Musa (peace be upon him), so that you may go to Pharaoh with confidence and armed with them. Hadrat Musa (peace be upon him) did not know that he had been chosen for this great mission and this great office. He knew who Pharaoh was, for he had already been in his household, and he was familiar with his arrogance and harsh oppression. Now, since he has come into the presence of the Lord of Honour, he understands that he has been granted a great honour and that he is a most noble servant. Thus the thought came into his heart that this was the suitable time to request the materials necessary for this mission at once, so that he might go to Pharaoh fully equipped.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verse 36:

He said: "You have been granted your request, O Musa (peace be upon him)!" (63)

Along with the acceptance of the request, there is also an expression of kindness and grace, of honour and respect, and then the affection of calling him by name, "O Musa." What greater honour could there be than that Allah, in the assembly of the whole universe, should name a servant and grant his requests?

Here you have seen how complete Allah's grace and favour has become; words of love and intimacy have passed. This state continued for a long time, supplication went on, all requests were accepted and fulfilled at once. Yet there is no gatekeeper over His favour, and no one can control Allah's mercies. Allah wishes to bestow further favour upon this servant, and by His pleasure He continues to extend this bounty for longer and longer. The time of his presence in this court is increased further. Now Allah wishes, by recounting His earlier blessings upon Musa (peace be upon him), to speak with him further, so that he may feel more reassured and become even more at ease. Allah begins to mention His mercies and His ancient kindnesses. The time of his meeting in this exalted court, whatever is added to it, is a treasure of life for him and a cause of pride. He is standing at a most radiant and sacred place. Listen:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verse 39:

﴿And I bestowed upon you love from Me﴾ (20:39) "I cast upon you love from Myself, and arranged that you be raised under My watchful care." O Almighty Lord, what wonders are Your power! All the forces of evil and rebellion turn to wax at the sight of him, and no one even looks at him with a malicious eye. Yet he is a weak infant, one who drinks milk, who cannot walk, cannot defend or protect himself, and cannot even speak.

In this picture two contrasting colors stand out. On one side is a mighty, compelling and rebellious power that is bent on killing this child. The atmosphere is so tense and harsh that on every side there is destruction, oppression, a coffin, waves and the sea. On the other side is a fine mantle of love that has been spread over this child. The mantle of love, this mantle of Allah's grace and kindness! It keeps shielding him from every danger: from the sea, from the coffin, from the violence of the waves, and even from the grip of rulers. Moses has no army or retinue; rather, the child has a natural attractiveness upon his face.

﴿And that you may be raised under My eye﴾ (20:39) "so that you be raised under My watchful care." Who can explain the meaning of this deep shelter of compassion and these wonders of the hand of divine power? The Qur'anic expression "that you be raised under My eyes" is an extraordinarily miraculous mode of expression. A human being is being raised in the eyes of Allah, and a human being is incapable of imagining the meanings behind this expression. It is a lofty station, a honor and dignity, that any person should obtain this gaze of mercy even for a moment. But observe the good fortune of this person: he is being raised under the watchful care of Another. This was the grace through which strength was created in Moses so that he could bear hardships and converse with Allah and derive guidance from that limitless Being.

﴿So that you may be raised under My eye.﴾ "Let you be raised under My eye. Let both of you be raised in the sight of Pharaoh, your enemy and the enemy of both of you, without any guard or protector, right within the hands of your enemy. Look, I did not even say that you should live comfortably in Pharaoh's house while your mother remains restless at home, afflicted with constant fear and anguish. I reunited the two of you.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (*Fi Zilal al-Quran*, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verses 40–41:

﴿When your sister walked along and said, "Shall I direct you to someone who will nurse him well?" Thus We returned you to your mother, that her eye might be cooled and she would not grieve.﴾ (02 : 04)

In this matter, it was God's plan that the child would not take the breast of any nursing woman. Pharaoh and his wife had adopted him as their son and were searching for a woman to nurse the child whom the river had cast onto the shore. People did not care for him, and Musa's (peace be upon him) sister, acting on a signal from her mother, said, "Shall I tell you of someone who will raise him well?" In this way his mother reached him, and he took her breast into his mouth. Thus God's plan reached its end: the mother who, through an inspired sign, had placed the child in a chest and set him adrift in the sea, and whose child the waves had thrown onto the shore, now had the child back in her lap. God took her child from the enemy and returned him to his mother. In this way, a secure arrangement for his upbringing was made. He was also saved from the danger of Pharaoh, who slaughtered the sons of Bani Israel and let the daughters live. The enemy himself was protecting him.

Another favour is in: ﴿And you killed a man, but We delivered you from distress and tested you with many trials, and you stayed for years among the people of Madyan. Then you came at the appointed time, O Musa. And I have chosen you for Myself.﴾ (02 : 04–14)

This happened when Musa had grown up in Pharaoh's palace. One day he was in the city when a dispute broke out between an Egyptian and an Israelite. The Israelite sought Musa's help, and in haste Musa struck the Egyptian with a fist. He did not intend to kill him; he only wanted to push him away. Musa was deeply grieved by this act, because he was walking under God's training, and his conscience reproached him that he had committed a sin. It is possible that God taught Musa *istighfar* (seeking forgiveness) at that time, and that the resentment was removed from his heart. Yet even so, God did not leave Musa without trial and affliction, because God had a great task for him. So He placed him in hardship: fear, leaving his homeland, and the struggle to escape *qisas* (legal retribution). He was put through the hardships of travel, separation from his family, and distance from his homeland. Then He gave him the difficult work of employment and of herding sheep. This was demanded of a man who had been raised in Pharaoh's royal palace, the great emperor of his age, with the luxuries of his court and every comfort in his house that ordinary people could not even imagine.

Then, at an appointed time, when his training was complete and he had matured, he had learned patience through these trials. He succeeded in the test, and conditions in Egypt became favourable for him. The oppression against Bani Israel reached its peak. At this appointed time God called Musa (peace be upon him) back from Madyan, although he thought that he was coming on his own.

﴿You stayed for years among the people of Madyan, then you came at the appointed time, O Musa.﴾

That is, at the time that I had set for you. I raised you under My own care, purely for Yourself, for My mission, and for the call. Therefore nothing in your life belongs to this world or to the next, apart from Me. All that you have comes from Me, and now you belong to My mission. Your upbringing, and now your mission, are also My mission. So you have no share in your own self, and no one else has a share in it, nor do your family and relatives. Therefore, for the sake of that for which I have trained you, and that mission for which I have prepared you, proceed now.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verses 42–44:

"Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and do not be remiss in remembering Me. Go, both of you, to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed (all bounds). And speak to him gently, perhaps he may be mindful or fear (Allah)."

You and your brother, go forth armed with My miracles. Of these miracles, the staff and the luminous hand have already been shown to you. Do not be remiss in My remembrance, for it is your important equipment in this field. It is your greatest weapon and support, and in times of difficulty it will be your refuge. Go to Pharaoh. Earlier, I had protected you from the evil of Pharaoh when you were a child, placed in a chest and cast into the sea, and the sea threw you onto the shore, so those hardships did you no harm. In those frightening circumstances you were not made to suffer. Now you go to that court fully prepared, and your brother is with you, so do not worry, for in such difficult situations too We have granted you deliverance.

Go to Pharaoh with the message, for he is a great rebel, a tyrant and a headstrong man.

"Then speak to him mildly" (20:44). This is because, in response to gentle speech, a person does not, thinking it an insult to himself, become stubborn. And rebels, given the false pride of the environment in which they live, do not become agitated. It is a property of gentle speech that it awakens hearts, and even a rebel becomes ready to reconsider his position because of gentle words.

Go to Pharaoh, and do not despair over whether he will ever come onto the path of guidance. Hope that he may benefit from admonition, and that fear of God may arise in his heart, for if a caller holds in his mind that the one to whom he goes can never come onto the path of guidance, then he cannot invite him with fervor, and if he refuses, he cannot continue the mission of da'wah with steadfastness.

God knew well what Pharaoh would answer, but it is necessary to call and to strive by every means for that purpose. God makes a practical decision about a person only when good or evil has actually proceeded from him, although God knows beforehand whether the outcome will be good or evil. God's knowledge of future events is like His knowledge of present events, or His knowledge of past events.

Until this point the address was to Musa (peace be upon him), and this scene was that of intimate conversation between the servant and the Worshipped in the valley of Tuwa. Now, within the context, the intervening events are folded in; the distances of time and place dissolve. Now both Musa and Harun are present. Before going to the court, both of them again express their apprehensions that difficulties may confront them in Pharaoh's court, and that perhaps, as soon as he hears their words, he may make some wrong decision, and when their words seem bitter to him, he may adopt rebellion.

**Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verse 45:**

"﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we..." ... "...upon whoever denies and turns away.﴾" (verses 54 to 84)

The long discussion that came before this, in which Musa (ʿalayhi al-salam) was speaking with his Lord in the valley of Tuwa, did not include Harun. It was a lengthy private supplication with extensive questions and answers. Therefore, the reply of both Musa and Harun,

﴿Indeed, we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress (20:45).﴾

"Both said, 'Our Lord, we fear that he will commit excess against us or will rush upon us.'" was not part of the supplication at the valley of Tuwa.

It is the Qur'an's method in its narratives (qasas, stories) to cut out the unnecessary parts from the middle and to leave a clear gap between the scenes it shows. The human intellect fills this gap itself, and the flow of the discourse or the scene moves forward and begins to present more effective, more beneficial, living and dynamic scenes, which have an impact on human conscience (wijdan).

It is evident that after returning from Mount Sinai, Musa (ʿalayhi al-salam) reached Egypt. Allah gave Harun the same office, and he was also commanded that you are a prophet who assists Musa. You too must go with your brother to invite Pharaoh. Now, when they are making their preparations to go, they express their apprehensions.

﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will commit excess against us or will rush upon us" (20:45).﴾

The lexical meaning of *farut* is that someone hastily harms another. They speak immediately, and the concept of *tughyan* (transgression) is more comprehensive than *farut* and harm. Pharaoh, in those days, was a tyrannical ruler from whom anything could be expected.

Here, a decisive reassurance is now given to them, after which there remains neither fear nor apprehension.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 20, verse 46:

Qal la takhafa inni ma'akuma asma'u wa ara (20:46) ["He said: Do not fear; indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing."] "Do not fear, I am with you. I hear everything and see everything." I am with you. Even if he (Pharaoh) is powerful, great and rebellious, Allah is the One who has control over all His servants.

Huwa al-Qahiru fawqa 'ibadih (He is the Subduer over His servants) [Qur'an 6:18]. He creates the entire universe, all humans, all animals and all things merely by "Kun" (Be). He needs to say nothing more than "Kun." "I am with you" is in itself a general reassurance and is sufficient. But Allah, to instill further tranquility and awareness in them, says:

Asma'u wa ara (20:46) ["I hear and I see."] What is Pharaoh? What does he possess? How could he commit oppression and rebellion? Allah is with you.

After giving this assurance, they are also taught the manner of calling (to the truth), and a concise form of invitation.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verses 47–48:

Verse 47–48 ("Go to him and say: We are the messengers of your Lord..." to "...and turns away")

"Go to him and say: We are the messengers of your Lord. Let the Children of Israel go with us and do not torment them. We have come to you with a sign from your Lord, and peace be upon the one who follows guidance. It has been revealed to us that punishment is for the one who denies and turns away."

From the very beginning, Allah explained what the mission of their messengership was.

"Indeed, we are the messengers of your Lord." In the first phrase it is made clear that there is another Being with you, a Lord who is the Lord of all people; He is not merely the God and Lord of Musa and Harun, nor is He only the Lord of the Children of Israel. This was the belief in the idolatrous superstitions of that time, that every nation has a lord and every tribe has its own god or deity, one or more. Even in the history of Egypt this notion persisted, that Pharaoh too was a lord, because he was of the lineage of the deities.

After this, the actual subject and content of their message is explained.

"So send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them." (20:47) Their real demand from Pharaoh was that you release the Children of Israel, that they may return to the belief in Tawhid, and return to the land which Allah has written for them, where they would dwell until they spread corruption in it and are utterly destroyed.

Now Pharaoh raised a new question.

He said: "What then is the case of the earlier generations?" (15)

"That is, what will become of those who passed away before your call? Where did they go? Who was their Lord? And they departed without any conception of that God about whom you speak."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verse 52:

قال علمها ……ينسى (25)

Moses (peace be upon him) left this second question of Pharaoh to Allah, because it related to the past. The summary of the answer is that Allah knows their state well; He has knowledge of everything and He never forgets. He is the One who knows all times, past or future. He knows the unseen, and Allah will also issue decrees concerning His servants.

After these answers, Moses introduces Allah further to Pharaoh before him: that He is the Sustainer of this universe, and what His blessings upon all people are. Thus some important signs from the cosmos and from the Egyptian environment are presented, because the land of Egypt was a green and flourishing land. Water there was abundant, and crops and livestock were plentiful.

﴿Who ... the people of understanding (35)﴾

Throughout all regions and all ages, the earth has been a cradle for human beings. It is a cradle in the same way that a cradle is for a child. Human beings stand upon the earth in the same way that children stand to their mother. The earth is a mother to all people. Its lap gives them shelter, and they eat their sustenance from its breast. Moreover, it has been prepared for them for rest, for travel, for cultivation, and for all the activities of life. Since Allah created everything with a nature (fitrat), from that day He has shaped it in this form. He gave the earth this form and condition so that it would be suitable (salih) for human life, because in Allah's plan human beings were to live here. Then, when He created the human being, He also made him in such a way that he would be ready to live on this earthly sphere, because Allah had prepared the earth for human beings and made it a cradle. The two meanings, mahd (meaning "prepared") and mahd (meaning "cradle"), are close to each other.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verses 55–56:

To complete Prophet Musa's statement, now comes this declaration of Allah:

Sayyid Qutb's commentary, Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation), on Surah 20, verse 57:

Qala aji'tana … duha (95)

Pharaoh did not engage in debate, nor did he answer an argument with an argument, because the proofs of Musa (peace be upon him) were strong. The proofs of Musa (peace be upon him) were connected with the signs of this universe, and also with the extraordinary miracles given to him. Instead, he resorted, like a defeated man, to a false accusation: that Musa had presented his staff as a serpent, and that this was clear sorcery. Furthermore, he said that Musa makes the hand white through sorcery. At that time sorcery was at its height in Egypt, so Pharaoh also made this accusation. These two miracles were such that they defeated sorcery, although sorcery is merely an illusion and a deception (takhyil). At most, the senses of those who see and hear are bewildered and deceived, and appearances are seen as though the reality of things has also changed, just as at times a person sees things that have no existence, or at times a person does not see things in the form that they actually have. A person affected by sorcery also sometimes shows such effects that a physical and nervous change is visible, but the reality does not change; whereas the miracles of Musa (peace be upon him) were such that reality itself changed. For a time, reality was completely transformed.

Qala aji'tana li-tukhrijana min ardina bi-sihrika ya Musa (20:57): "He said: O Musa, have you come to us so that by the power of your magic you drive us out of our land?" This shows that in Egypt the Children of Israel were enslaved as a political measure, because they were very numerous and their population was growing. When the question of power arises, tyrannical rulers become ready to inflict ever more severe torment upon the people. They inflict sufferings on human beings for which no justification exists in any human conception, and such violence is against the human conscience, human dignity and human rights. This is why Pharaoh would kill the sons of the Children of Israel, keep the daughters alive, and take forced labour from them, and of the hardest kind. When Musa and Harun (peace be upon them both) made the demand:

Arsil ma'ana Bani Isra'il wa la tu'adhdhibhum: "Send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them," he responded with this accusation.

Qala aji'tana li-tukhrijana min ardina bi-sihrika ya Musa (20:57): "Musa, you come to us so that by your magic you drive us out of our land." Because the freedom and migration of the Children of Israel meant, in his view, that they might attack and take possession of Egypt.

When, in his thinking, Musa (peace be upon him) wishes to free the Children of Israel merely by the power of magic, the natural response is that we too will bring the same kind of magic.

"Then We will surely bring you a magic like it." Those who rebel and irreligious leaders have always thought that those who call to the truth actually seek supreme power in the country. Their call is in fact a veil behind which they carry out revolutionary work. After this, when they see that the caller (da'i, one who invites to faith) has proofs and evidence, or miracles like those of Musa (peace be upon him), or arguments that enter the heart like magic, then tyrannical rulers provide themselves with such arguments. Magic against magic, speech against speech, reform against reform, good deeds against good deeds. But they do not know that the people of truth have faith, and against faith they have no faith. Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verse 60:

﴿So Pharaoh withdrew and gathered his schemes, then came back.﴾

The Qur'an has left out Pharaoh's instructions, the consultations of Pharaoh's chiefs, and the dialogue that took place between him and the sorcerers. Here the Qur'an omits all the events that followed the contest with the sorcerers. Leaving aside all these events, the scene now shown is that of outward victory, so that after the victory of the heart and of conviction, the victory on the battlefield may be shown, and the help and support of God may become visible to the believers with their own eyes: complete and decisive victory. For this reason, before this scene, the scenes of the Children of Israel's departure and their standing before the sea have not been prolonged, unlike the way these scenes are presented in detail in other surahs. Rather, after a few glimpses, complete victory is set before us, because the human mind can itself imagine all these omitted scenes, and so they are left to the imagination.

Musa (peace be upon him) was commanded to take My servants and leave by night. A dry path would be found for them in the sea, and Pharaoh's armies would not be able to seize them. Do not fear the dry paths made in the sea either, for God has kept the water of the sea according to a law, and He can, for a while, turn it away from its natural course. Acting upon these instructions, when Musa set out:

﴿فَأَتْبَعَهُمْ...وَمَا هَدَىٰ﴾ (98) (02:88–98) "Pharaoh followed them with his armies, and then the sea covered them, as covering was due to them. Pharaoh had led his people astray, and had given them no right guidance."

Here the Qur'an also mentions Pharaoh's drowning only briefly. The details are not given, so that this event remains summary. Throughout his life Pharaoh led his people in immorality, wickedness and error, and now, at the time of ruin and destruction, he led his people into the sea. Just as the Qur'an has deliberately left this link of the event summarized for a particular wisdom, we too shall leave it summarized. It is appropriate that we discuss the lessons we derive from this scene and the effect that its events have on hearts.

The first lesson in this story is that the hand of divine power has set faith and rebellion face to face and has arranged a contest between them. In this contest, the believers were asked only to keep obeying the commands. They were told to set out by night, because between the two fronts there was no balance of military strength. If one examines the situation realistically, there was no comparison between these two powers. Musa (peace be upon him) and his people were weak, and had no material power, whereas Pharaoh and his armies possessed every kind of power. Therefore there was no opportunity for a material war between them, and so divine power took this battle into its own hands. But when faith became firm in the hearts of the believers, when faith had entered their hearts deeply, and when they had no other material power than this, the power of faith spoke to an arrogant absolute ruler eye to eye. It did not fear his threats and gave no regard to the wealth and honour possessed by those in authority. The rebellious dictator said:

﴿لَأُقَطِّعَنَّ أَيْدِيَكُم وَأَرْجُلَكُم مِّنْ خِلَافٍ وَلَأُصَلِّبَنَّكُمْ فِي جُذُوعِ النَّخْلِ﴾ (18) "I will cut off your hands and feet from opposite sides, and I will crucify you on the trunks of palm trees." In reply they said:

﴿فَاقْضِ مَا أَنتَ قَاضٍ ۖ إِنَّمَا تَقْضِي هَٰذِهِ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا﴾ (02:28) "Then decide whatever you wish to decide; you can only decide the matter of this worldly life." When the contest in the field of hearts, between ideological and faithful strength and the strength of arrogance and authority, reached this point, then divine power raised the banner of faith so that it might exalt it, and the banner of the people of falsehood was lowered, without the people of truth making any material struggle for it.

The second lesson is that as long as the Children of Israel kept paying Pharaoh the tax of humiliation and slavery, while their sons were slain and their daughters were left alive, divine power did not rise to their aid, and this battle was not made to take place. This was because they paid that tax merely out of humiliation, slavery and fear. But when faith rose high in their hearts, and they decided to bear the difficulties and oppression in the way of faith, when they began to walk with their heads held high, when they began to raise the word of truth, to speak to Pharaoh eye to eye, and when they did all this while facing every kind of dangerous risk, then divine power rose to help them. This battle began at a time when, before the victory on the battlefield, the believers had already triumphed in the world of the heart.

Through this summary, the Qur'an here wishes to give this very lesson and teaching, and in these scenes no detailed particulars have been given, so that those who carry the call of Islam may know when God's help will come to them, and when victory will be granted to them against rebels and transgressors.

When the Children of Israel were stepping into a free atmosphere, raising the banners of victory and help, they are now admonished, reminded of the lesson of truth, and warned of an evil end, so that they do not forget the lesson that is derived from the conflict between Pharaoh and Musa. Now let the atmosphere of freedom and power not put them into pride and arrogance, and let them not ignore the equipment that, despite the imbalance of power, made them victorious, for this true strength, the strength of faith, is the guarantor of victory in every field.

Yet even for this most recent blessing, the Lord draws their attention, so that you do not forget this event. Reflect and be thankful.

The promise made with the Children of Israel at Mount Tur, mentioned here, has already taken place. After their exodus from Egypt, Musa (peace be upon him) was called by Allah at Tur, so that he might be trained for meeting with Allah, and so that he might hear from Allah the teachings that were to be given to him on the Tablets, which related to religion and Shariah, and so that the Children of Israel might be prepared and organized for the role of conduct they were to carry out in the Holy Land.

Then the sending down of Manna and Salwa for them: Manna was a sweet substance which gathered on the leaves of trees, and Salwa was a bird which gathered for them in large numbers in the desert, and could be easily caught and eaten. These two things were a special favour for them in that barren plain and uninhabited desert. These things were provided to them as their daily food, and were provided with great ease.

Allah reminds the Children of Israel of these favours and advises them: eat of them, but do not transgress, and do not become lost in luxury and comfort so as to forget the aims and the purpose for which you left Egypt. What they are especially being forbidden here is transgression. They had already seen transgression in Egypt; they had already endured its oppressions under it, and had also already seen its outcome.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verse 81:

﴿Do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you; and whoever has My wrath descend upon him has indeed fallen.﴾ (20:81)

"Do not be insolent, for otherwise My wrath will fall upon you, and whoever upon whom My wrath falls has certainly fallen and been ruined."

Only recently they had seen how Pharaoh fell. He fell from his throne, and then he fell into the sea. Just as falling shows the movement from above to below, so insolence and arrogance show the movement from below to above. The Qur'an, in its particular manner of expression, presents these two things linked together, in which meanings stand in opposition to one another.

This warning and threat is addressed to the people who had recently left Egypt for a specific purpose, lest freedom and love of luxury lead them astray. They should not become weak by adopting a life of luxury. But alongside this warning and threat, the door of repentance also remains open, so that if anyone makes a mistake, he may return.

﴿And indeed, I am Most Forgiving toward one who repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then remains on guidance.﴾ (02 : 28) "Indeed I am Most Forgiving to whoever repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then follows the right path." It should be remembered that repentance is not merely a word that one utters, but the name of a resolve of the heart. Its meaning is determined only through faith and righteous deeds, and it becomes manifest in the real world through human conduct. If a person repents, his faith is sound, and his deeds confirm it, then only can he be called a person who has been guided, a person who is a guarantor of guidance and righteous deeds. In short, when there is no guidance after repentance, that is, no practical change, then repentance has no meaning.

Until now we have been witnessing the success of the Children of Israel and the commentary and admonition upon it. Now the curtain falls, and in the next scene we see Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) conversing with Allah on Mount Tur.

Allah had promised Musa (peace be upon him) that he would spend forty days on Tur and, after that, converse with Allah and receive commands from Him, that is, the commands for achieving victory after defeat. Achieving victory also has its requirements. Every ideology has some requirements. Likewise, receiving commands requires psychological preparation and developing capacity within oneself, and this was also necessary. Musa climbed the mountain, left the people below, and appointed Harun (peace be upon him) as his deputy among them.

Musa (peace be upon him) had an extremely strong longing for this meeting. Presenting himself before Allah was a great honour, and he was eager for it. Previously he had already tasted the sweetness of speaking with Allah. Therefore, with great longing, he hastened and reached Tur. He stood before Allah, but he did not know what his people had done after him, because he had left them at the foot of the mountain.

Here, the Lord tells Musa (peace be upon him) what the Children of Israel have done after him. Let us look at the scene and listen to the conversation:

Moses (peace be upon him) was astonished on hearing this. He was eager for the meeting with his Lord. He had already completed the forty days and had also made preparations for the meeting, so that he might obtain a new system of life for the Children of Israel, for he had only just been freed from the slavery of Pharaoh under his leadership. The aim was that the Children of Israel should become a nation that possessed a message and bore certain obligations.

But the condition of the Children of Israel was such that a long life of humiliation and the slavery of idol-worshipping Pharaonism had changed their conscience. They were not able to bear hardship. They could neither be patient in difficulties nor remain steadfast in any covenant or agreement. Slavery, imitation and love of ease had taken deep root in their consciousness. As soon as Moses left them under the supervision of Harun (Aaron) and moved away from them even a little, their beliefs changed, and at the very first trial they collapsed completely. For them, continuous testing was necessary, and it was necessary to repeatedly place them in continuous hardships and trials so that their psychological training could be carried out. The worship of the calf was their first trial; it was an artificial calf that the Samiri (al-Samiri) had made for them.

He had already completed the forty days and had also made preparations for the meeting, so that he might obtain a new system of life for the Children of Israel, for he had only just been freed from the slavery of Pharaoh under his leadership. But the condition of the Children of Israel was such that a long life of humiliation and the slavery of idol-worshipping Pharaonism had changed their conscience. They were not able to bear hardship. They could neither be patient in difficulties nor remain steadfast in any covenant or agreement. Slavery, imitation and love of ease had taken deep root in their consciousness. As soon as Moses left them under the supervision of Harun (Aaron) and moved away from them even a little, their beliefs changed, and at the very first trial they collapsed completely. Moses (peace be upon him) had no knowledge of this trial. He first learned of it during his meeting with Allah. Moses took these tablets. In them was guidance, a code for building the life of the Children of Israel, given to prepare them for the purpose for which they had been raised up.

Here the scene of Moses' communion on Mount Sinai is quickly folded up, so that the impressions that came over Moses on hearing the news of his people's deviation may be recorded. His haste to return appears in the scene, and it is shown how greatly he was filled with anger and indignation. It was only recently that he had freed this people from the slavery of Pharaoh and delivered them from the disgrace of idol worship. Then Allah provided them with food and drink in the wilderness, gave them clear instructions, warned them to avoid misguidance, and also explained the consequences and results of going astray. Yet their condition was such that at the very first call they became idol worshippers, and then they engaged in worshipping the artificial calf.

Here the Qur'an does not explicitly state whether Allah had informed Moses in detail of the misguidance of the Children of Israel. But Moses' expression of anger upon his return, his being extremely displeased, his being angry with his brother, and his rebuke of the people all indicate that Allah had told him everything, and that he knew the Children of Israel had committed a most wicked act.

Harun had already told them, before Musa came back: "O my people, you are being tested by this, for your Lord is the Most Merciful. So follow me and obey my command." But they replied: "We will not cease to be devoted to it until Musa returns to us."

This is the trial through which the Children of Israel went astray. However, the Qur'an mentions it at the time when Musa (peace be upon him) comes before his people and makes an inquiry. Before this, during the occasion of his intimate conversation with Allah, the Qur'an did not disclose it. These details were kept hidden so that they might be revealed at the time when Musa (peace be upon him) himself conducted the investigation.

When Musa (peace be upon him) returned, he saw that his people were worshipping an artificial calf that produced a sound. This calf was made of gold. Moreover, these people were saying: "This is your god and the god of Musa." Musa had gone away by mistake to Mount Sinai to meet his Lord, whereas your Lord is truly present before you!

When Musa (peace be upon him) came, in a state of extreme anger, he began to question them:

"O my people, did your Lord not make you a good promise?" (20:86) Allah had promised them that if they remained steadfast upon the belief in Tawhid, they would enter the Holy Land and would be granted victory. Not too long had passed since that covenant and the appearance of its signs. Then he rebuked them severely.

"Did the time seem long to you, or did you want the anger of your Lord to descend upon you?" (20:86) Because your conduct is such that it shows you desire the wrath of Allah; it is as though you did this deliberately and intentionally sought the wrath of Allah. Had a very long time passed?

"So you broke your promise to me." (20:86) You had promised that until my return you would remain faithful to my covenant, and that you would make no change in your beliefs or actions without my permission.

Now consider their excuse: it shows that prolonged enslavement had corrupted their hearts and vision, and that their minds were not functioning properly either.

ما اخلقنا موعدک بملکنا (02 : 88) "We did not break our promise to you of our own accord. The matter was so great that it was not within our power to refrain from it."

These were the ornaments of Egyptian women which they had brought with them. It is to this burden that they refer. We threw these ornaments away to lighten the load, because they were with us and they were unlawful (haram). The Samiri took them and made from them this calf. The Samiri was a native of Egypt who had become their companion; or he was a man from among the Children of Israel who had adopted this title. He had made holes in the calf such that when air passed through them, a sound like the lowing of a calf would come out. The calf had neither life nor spirit, for it was a lifeless body, and that is what is called a body in which there is no life. As soon as they saw the calf making a sound, they forgot the God who had delivered them from Egypt, that is, from the land of humiliation. So they began to worship this golden calf. Because of their foolishness and lack of understanding, they began to say:

The Lord of you all is Allah, and the Lord of Musa. Musa is seeking Him on the mountain, while He is here with us, and Musa has forgotten the path to his Lord.

This is a matter that reveals both their foolishness and their lack of understanding, and it also shows how easily they level accusations against their Prophet under whose leadership, and under whose protection and watchful care, they had just been delivered, and by whose freedom they gained exactly in accordance with Allah's instructions. In such circumstances, their charge against Hadrat Musa (peace be upon him), that he has no connection with his Lord, that he has lost the way and has not been able to reach his Lord, is a very great audacity on their part. But they were the Children of Israel.

They are presenting this as an excuse, though in reality it is a clear deception on their part.

It appears that Hadrat Harun was a man of calm temperament, who kept his emotions under control in comparison to Hadrat Musa. He seeks a sensitive point in Hadrat Musa's consciousness. Kinship is a sensitive bond. According to his own view, he presents the excuse that if I had acted according to your instructions, there would have been a split among the Bani Israel: one group would have risen in support of the calf, and the other would have joined me, whereas your command was that you should guard and watch over the Bani Israel and not allow any new matter to arise among them. So, saving them from disunity is also obedience to the command.

Hadrat Musa's anger and wrath then turns towards the Samiri, who had invented this trial. Earlier, Hadrat Musa did not turn to him because it was also the duty of the people not to obey just anyone and everyone. Then comes the responsibility of Hadrat Harun, because he too was responsible to block the path of those who worshipped the calf. As for the Samiri, his responsibility comes last, because he had not forced them to worship the calf, nor had he placed a seal upon their intellect. He misled them, and they became ready to be misled. It was within their power to obey their first Prophet, and then it was their duty to act upon the advice of the second Prophet. Therefore, the primary responsibility lies with the people first, then with their overseer, and after that with the person who created this trial. Hence Hadrat Musa turned to him last.

Samiri, tell us what you did and why you did it?

This phrasing indicates that Samiri committed some very grave offence.

Commentary on the answer of the Samiri, there are various opinions and narrations. What did he see that others did not see? Who was that Messenger whose footprint he took a handful from and threw? Then, what is the connection of that act with the making of the calf? What effects did that dust have on the calf?

In most of these narrations it is said that the Samiri saw Jibra'il (peace be upon him) in the form in which he descends to the earth, and he picked up dust from beneath his feet. Or, he picked up dust from beneath the hooves of his horse and placed it upon the calf made of gold, and a sound began to come from it. Or, that dust turned a heap of gold into a calf.

The Qur'an has not explained the reality of this event here. The Qur'an has only related the statement of the Samiri. We understand that this was an excuse of the Samiri, a fabricated pretext which he invented so that he might escape the consequences of his action. The calf was indeed made from the gold which the Children of Israel had brought with them from Egypt, and then he had thrown it. The Samiri described it in such a manner that the wind would produce from it a sound like the sound of a calf. After this he mentioned the dust of the traces of the Messenger, so that he might give his act the colour of sanctity and attach this matter to the footprint of the Messenger.

Whatever the reality may be, Hadrat Musa (peace be upon him) expelled him from the community of the Children of Israel. He banished him for his whole life and left his matter to Allah in the Hereafter. Musa (peace be upon him) treated the Samiri harshly in the matter of this artificial deity, and adopted such an attitude towards the deity as well, so that people might see that this deity did not even help its maker.

You are on the Tahir side? No, let me just translate.

Go, you are outcast, and no one shall touch you, neither with good nor with evil, and you shall not touch anyone. In the religion of Musa (peace be upon him), this was one of the punishments. It was a punishment of making one untouchable, and the offender was declared impure, so that he could not touch anyone, and no one could touch him. As for ﴿that for you there is an appointed time for reckoning﴾, the meaning here is the Day of Resurrection, the time of recompense and punishment, from which, even if one wishes to escape, one cannot escape. After this, Musa spoke these commands with great severity and anger: take this calf, burn it, and scatter its ashes into the sea. Severity and anger are part of the temperament of Musa (peace be upon him). Here his severity and anger are solely for Allah, and anger in matters of Allah's religion is not blameworthy. Severity in matters of religion is regarded as praiseworthy.

When the god of the Samiri was seen burning before them, Musa considered it appropriate, in the face of that scene, to tell the people the truth about the Islamic belief and about the god.

The passage ends the section on the story of Musa (peace be upon him) in this surah, after this clarification about Islamic belief. This story shows that the bearers of the Islamic call receive the rains of Allah's mercy from every direction, even if some error occurs from them at the beginning. After this, the other stages of the story are left out here. The events that follow show that the Children of Israel commit acts of disobedience, and one punishment after another comes upon them. Since the theme here is mercy, kindness and favours, and these mercies are bestowed upon the righteous servants of Allah, the links of the story that mention the disobedience of the Children of Israel have been omitted here, because mentioning them is contrary to the theme, subject matter and atmosphere of the surah. For this reason the story has been concluded at this point.

Lesson No. 931 — At a Glance

At the beginning of the surah, the subject under discussion was the Qur'an: that it was not revealed to the Messenger ﷺ so that he should be put into hardship because of it. After that, the story of Musa (peace be upon him) was taken up to establish how much Allah shows consideration to His servants and messengers, and how much favour He bestows upon them, as He did upon Musa, his brother, and his people.

Now, after this lengthy story, commentary is offered here, and the subject returns to the Qur'an. It is explained what the purpose of the Qur'an's revelation is, and what will be the end of those who turn away from it. Presenting one of the scenes of the Resurrection, it is shown that the days and nights of the world will shrink, the mountains will be lifted off the face of the earth, and it will be left bare — just a levelled plain. People will stand in the place of assembly, awe-struck, and all faces will be bowed and humbled before the Living, the Self-Subsisting (Al-Hayy Al-Qayyum). The purpose of this scene, and of all those scenes of the Qur'an in which people are warned, is solely to instil the fear of Allah in people's hearts.

In the context of the discussion of the Qur'an, the Messenger ﷺ is also given the assurance that he will not forget the Qur'an. He is told not to hasten in repeating it out of fear of forgetting it, and not to bring hardship upon himself because of it. Allah will make it easy for him, and he will be enabled to memorise it. He should simply keep praying: "My Lord, increase me in knowledge."

When revelation was descending, the Prophet ﷺ would begin repeating the words of the Qur'an before the revelation had finished, out of fear that he might forget them. He was given reassurance regarding this, but in keeping with the theme, it was explained that Adam (peace be upon him) had forgotten his covenant. Iblis had caused him to forget, and therefore a deep-rooted enmity has continued between Adam and Iblis. Among the descendants of Adam, some people forget their covenant, while others remember it; and this outcome too is presented as one of the scenes of the Resurrection. It is, as it were, the conclusion of a journey that began from the higher realm and also ends with a return to the higher realm.

The surah concludes with the message that O Messenger, do not be distressed on account of those who deny the call or turn away from it. Such people have been given a limited time in this world. The provisions and the abundant worldly goods given to them during that limited time are no benefit to them; rather, they are a trial and a test for them. You are also advised to turn your attention to the worship of Allah and to His remembrance; in this way you will attain more contentment than the wealth of any rich person, and you will be satisfied with your own condition. Before this, Allah destroyed many nations by putting them to trial in this same manner. Allah has completed the proof against the people by sending to them the Prophet of the last age and the final Messenger. Now the people have no excuse for not believing. Therefore, you should withdraw your hand from concern about their end, leave it to Allah, and say:

"Qul kullun mutarabbisun fatarabbasu fasata'lamun man ashabus-sirat-is-sawiyyi wa man ihtada" (20:135) — "Say, O Muhammad, to them: each one is awaiting the outcome; so wait, and soon you will know who are on the even path and who are rightly guided."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verse 103:

The stories that are being revealed to you are accounts of past events. The Qur'an mentions them. The Qur'an has been described from this perspective. These stories are in reality also the remembrance of God (dhikr Ilahi) and the signs of God (ayat Ilahi), and they also mention the signs of God that appeared in earlier centuries.

Those who turn away from this remembrance are addressed here as the criminals (mujrimin). A scene of them is presented here. They have carried heavy burdens, just as a traveler carries his load. But there is nothing beneficial for them in this burden. When the Trumpet is blown, on that day the faces of the criminals will turn blue, that is, they will appear blue from fear and from extreme grief. They will speak to one another in whispers. Because of the terror that pervades the atmosphere and the awe of the Day of Resurrection, they will not speak loudly. They will be speaking softly. Their talk will be about the days they spent on earth. In their perception and consciousness, the whole span of the worldly era will appear so shrunken and brief that the entire life, or the whole human age on earth, will appear as no more than a few days.

"In labithtum illa 'ashra" (20:103 as cited by the author, reference 02:301): "You will have spent perhaps ten days." Among them, the one who is most sound in judgment will estimate even less, that it was only a single day's life.

﴿Ilia labithtum illa yawman﴾ (02 : 301), "You did not remain [in the world] except for a day." The long lives of this worldly existence will appear to them extremely brief. The pleasures they indulged in during life will look like sorrows, and the time will appear very short, and worthless in terms of value. For what is the worth of ten nights, however full of luxury and ease they may have been? And what is the worth of a single night, even if each of its minutes was filled with good fortune? Compared with the unbounded time of eternity, and the days of abiding in which these people are now going, after reckoning, to dwell forever in Hell, what value can either of these have?

From this terrifying scene of the Resurrection, we are brought back again to the world, and the question is raised: what will happen to these mountains on the Day of Resurrection? They see the mountains as merely lying there. Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verse 114:

He is Allah, supremely exalted, before whom faces bow down. Those who bear wrong will indeed be disappointed in His presence, but for the believers who do righteous deeds there is perfect tranquillity. He sends down this Qur'an from the heights, so do not be hasty with it before its revelation is completed. The revelation of the Qur'an contains profound wisdom, and this wisdom and purpose will surely be fulfilled. So continue to ask your Lord for increase in knowledge, and be content with what is being given to you. Do not show anxiety that it will be taken away from you. Knowledge is indeed that which is in Allah's knowledge. It remains, it will always benefit, it will endure, it will keep flourishing and will never be lost.

In this connection, that is, in relation to the theme of knowledge and forgetfulness, the story of Adam comes here. Adam was told: dwell in the Garden and do not approach this tree. He fell for the deception of Satan, who claimed that this was the Tree of Eternity, and so he ate of it. Before being granted the caliphate on earth, this was a trial from the Lord for him, and Allah caused Adam to undergo this experience so that it might be a lesson for the humans who would come after him. When this trial was completed, Allah's mercy came, Adam was chosen, and he was shown the right path.

Wherever the stories of the Qur'an appear, there is a specific purpose for bringing them in the context of the discourse. This story comes here after the event in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to hasten in receiving the divine revelation out of fear of forgetting. Here, in the story of Adam too, it is said that Adam's error occurred because of forgetfulness. Moreover, the entire theme of the surah is that Allah, the Exalted, has His special regard for the servants whom He selects for the call to Islam, and upon them showers of mercy and compassion fall. Thus it is shown that when Adam erred through forgetfulness, Allah showed mercy to him and gave him guidance. After this, a glimpse from the scenes of the Day of Resurrection comes, in which the condition of the obedient is described, as well as the condition of the disobedient: that Adam descends to the earth, and after standing, returns to the original station and presents an account.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 20, verse 115:

For the training of a human being and for testing his willpower, it is necessary that he be forbidden certain things, so that his personality becomes firm.
